questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests CKAD basics in a slightly different data path: file-based ingestion, ConfigMap-driven batching, and integrating InitContainers, Secrets, TLS sidecars, and networking policies in a realistic per-namespace pattern. It also probes how a candidate balances durability vs. simplicity in a beginner task.

## Key Concepts
- ConfigMapKeyRef for BATCH_SIZE
- PVC-based volumes and multi-moint approach
- InitContainer provisioning (python3, watchdog)
- Sidecar for TLS/certs
- Secrets for credentials
- Readiness/Liveness probes
- Namespace NetworkPolicy to restrict egress

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: log-collector-config
data:
  BATCH_SIZE: "100"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: log-portal-creds
type: Opaque
data:
  username: <base64>
  password: <base64>
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: log-collector
spec:
  replicas: 1
  template:
    spec:
      initContainers:
      - name: installer
        image: alpine:3.18
        command: ["sh","-c","apk add --no-cache python3 py3-pip && pip3 install watchdog"]
      containers:
      - name: watcher
        image: my-registry/log-watcher:latest
        volumeMounts:
        - mountPath: /logs
          name: logs
        - mountPath: /summaries
          name: summaries
        env:
        - name: BATCH_SIZE
          valueFrom:
            configMapKeyRef:
              name: log-collector-config
              key: BATCH_SIZE
      volumes:
      - name: logs
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: logs-pvc
      - name: summaries
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: summaries-pvc
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you modify this to ensure at-least-once delivery of the digest? 
- What changes would you make to support multiple namespaces scaling this pattern effectively?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked

Tests CKAD fundamentals for per-namespace automation, using CronJobs, ConfigMaps, Secrets, InitContainers, and PVC-backed logs in a realistic heartbeat scenario.

## Key Concepts

- CronJob scheduling and Job templates
- ConfigMap and Secret usage for config and creds
- InitContainer for one-time setup
- Probes for container health
- PersistentVolumeClaim for logs

## Code Example

```javascript
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: heartbeat-cron
  namespace: default
spec:
  schedule: "*/10 * * * *"
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          initContainers:
          - name: install-deps
            image: alpine:3.19
            command: ["sh","-c","apk add --no-cache curl"]
          containers:
          - name: heartbeater
            image: alpine:3.19
            command: ["sh","-c","curl -sS -X POST -H \"Authorization: Bearer $API_TOKEN\" $TARGET_URL/heartbeat -d '{\"ts\": \"$(date +%s)\"}'"]
            envFrom:
            - configMapRef:
                name: cron-config
            - secretRef:
                name: target-creds
            volumeMounts:
            - name: logs
              mountPath: /logs
            readinessProbe:
              exec:
                command: ["sh","-c","test -f /logs/ready"]
              initialDelaySeconds: 5
              periodSeconds: 10
            livenessProbe:
              httpGet:
                path: /healthz
                port: 80
              initialDelaySeconds: 15
              periodSeconds: 20
          restartPolicy: OnFailure
          volumes:
          - name: logs
            persistentVolumeClaim:
              claimName: heartbeat-logs
```

## Follow-up Questions

- How would you rotate the API token without recreating the CronJob?
- What failure modes and retries would you implement?

## Why This Is Asked
Tests practical CKAD wiring: PVC usage, InitContainer tooling, manifest validation, per-namespace health aggregation, internal POST, and network isolation.

## Key Concepts
- InitContainer for tooling setup and pre-flight checks
- PVC mounting and runtime manifest processing
- Sidecar for TLS rotation
- Probes for reliability
- Secrets for credentials
- Namespace NetworkPolicy for egress control

## Code Example
```yaml
# minimal skeleton
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: health-agg
  namespace: ckad
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: health-agg
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: health-agg
    spec:
      volumes:
        - name: manifests
          persistentVolumeClaim:
            claimName: svc-manifests-pvc
        - name: tls
          secret:
            secretName: tls-secret
      initContainers:
        - name: prep
          image: alpine:3.18
          command: ["sh", "-c", "apk add --no-cache curl jq curl && kubeval /svc-manifests/*.yaml || true"]
          volumeMounts:
            - name: manifests
              mountPath: /svc-manifests
      containers:
        - name: health-agg
          image: myorg/health-agg:latest
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
          volumeMounts:
            - name: manifests
              mountPath: /svc-manifests
        - name: tls-sidecar
          image: myorg/tls-sidecar:latest
          volumeMounts:
            - name: tls
              mountPath: /tls
      readinessProbe:
        httpGet:
          path: /health
          port: 8080
        initialDelaySeconds: 5
        periodSeconds: 10
      livenessProbe:
        httpGet:
          path: /health
          port: 8080
        initialDelaySeconds: 15
        periodSeconds: 20
```

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
This question tests knowledge of namespace-scoped governance primitives (LimitRange, ResourceQuota) and how defaults affect scheduling, QoS, and multi-tenant fairness in CKAD.

## Key Concepts
- Namespace scoping
- LimitRange defaultRequests/defaultLimits
- ResourceQuota hard limits
- Pod scheduling under quotas
- Impact on autoscaling and experimentation

## Code Example
```yaml
# Namespace
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: test-ns
---
# LimitRange
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata:
  name: default-limits
  namespace: test-ns
spec:
  limits:
  - default:
      cpu: 200m
      memory: 256Mi
    defaultRequest:
      cpu: 100m
      memory: 128Mi
    type: Container
---
# ResourceQuota
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: resource-quota
  namespace: test-ns
spec:
  hard:
    pods: "10"
    requests.cpu: "1"
    requests.memory: 1Gi
    limits.cpu: "2"
    limits.memory: 2Gi
---
# Deployment (inherits defaults)
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: sample-app
  namespace: test-ns
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: sample-app
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: sample-app
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: app
        image: nginx:latest
```

## Trade-offs
**Advantages:**
- Prevents resource starvation across namespaces
- Enforces fair resource distribution
- Automatic defaults reduce configuration errors
- Provides cost control boundaries

**Considerations:**
- Too restrictive limits can hinder scaling
- Default limits may be overprovisioned for small workloads
- ResourceQuota refusals require manual quota increases
- May impact autoscaling behavior if quotas are too tight

**Best Practices:**
- Set conservative defaults but allow overrides
- Monitor quota utilization regularly
- Use separate quotas for production vs development
- Consider pod priority classes for critical workloads

## Why This Is Asked

- PVC mounts and tar packaging

- Secret-based credentials for remote backups
- Readiness/Liveness probes
- Namespace NetworkPolicy egress controls

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: ns-backup
spec:
  schedule: "0 2 * * *"
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          initContainers:
            - name: installer
              image: busybox
              command:
                - /bin/sh
                - -c
                - apk add --no-cache tar pigz
          containers:
            - name: backup
              image: alpine:3.18
              command:
                - /bin/sh
                - -c
                - tar -czf /backup/namespace-$(date +%F-%H%M).tar.gz -C /data .
              volumeMounts:
                - name: data
                  mountPath: /data
                - name: backup
                  mountPath: /backup
              readinessProbe:
```

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
This question tests CKAD competencies including per-namespace controller patterns, ConfigMap/Secret integration, Deployment patching, RBAC configuration, and operational pause/resume with cooldown logic. It also validates understanding of observability through PVC-based logging and InitContainer provisioning.

## Key Concepts
- **Per-namespace controller design**: Controller runs within the target namespace rather than cluster-wide
- **RBAC**: ClusterRole with namespaced patch permissions for Deployments
- **ConfigMap/Secret integration**: Canary policy and credentials consumed as volumes or environment variables
- **Patch-based control flow**: Annotation-driven pause/resume mechanism
- **PVC-based logging**: Persistent storage for diagnostic data
- **NetworkPolicy**: Namespace-scoped egress restrictions to monitoring endpoints

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: canary-policy
data:
  threshold: "0.8"
  cooldown: "300"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: metrics-credentials
type: Opaque
stringData:
  api_key: ""
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: canary-controller
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: canary-controller
rules:
- apiGroups: ["apps"]
  resources: ["deployments"]
  verbs: ["get", "list", "watch", "patch"]
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["configmaps", "secrets"]
  verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: canary-controller
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: canary-controller
  template:
    spec:
      serviceAccountName: canary-controller
      initContainers:
      - name: installer
        image: busybox
        command: ["sh", "-c", "apk add --no-cache curl jq"]
        volumeMounts:
        - name: logs
          mountPath: /logs
      containers:
      - name: controller
        image: canary-controller:latest
        volumeMounts:
        - name: logs
          mountPath: /logs
        - name: policy
          mountPath: /config
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /ready
            port: 8080
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health
            port: 8080
      volumes:
      - name: logs
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: canary-logs
      - name: policy
        configMap:
          name: canary-policy
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: canary-egress
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: canary-controller
  policyTypes: ["Egress"]
  egress:
  - to:
    - podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: prometheus
```

## Trade-offs

| Aspect | Consideration |
|--------|---------------|
| **Per-namespace vs Cluster-wide** | Simpler RBAC and isolation, but requires separate Deployment per namespace |
| **Annotation-based pausing** | Non-invasive but relies on controller availability |
| **PVC for logs** | Provides persistence but requires storage provisioning |
| **InitContainer approach** | Increases pod startup time; consider sidecar pattern for production |
| **Polling vs Events** | Simple polling is easier to implement; watch API is more efficient but complex |

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
This question validates understanding of per-namespace resource governance in Kubernetes. It tests knowledge of how LimitRange and ResourceQuota work together to control pod sizing and cluster resource allocation.

## Key Concepts
- **LimitRange**: Sets default requests/limits applied to Pods that don't specify resources
- **ResourceQuota**: Enforces hard limits on total namespace resource consumption
- **Policy alignment**: Ensuring Deployments specify resources matching namespace defaults
- **Verification**: Testing policy enforcement with intentional over-allocation
- **Rollback**: Strategy for removing or scaling back resources when policies need adjustment

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata:
  name: analytics-lr
  namespace: analytics
spec:
  limits:
  - type: Container
    default:
      cpu: "200m"
      memory: 256Mi
    defaultRequest:
      cpu: "100m"
      memory: 128Mi
```
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: analytics-quo
  namespace: analytics
spec:
  hard:
    cpu: "400m"
    memory: 512Mi
    requests.storage: "1Gi"
```
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: reporter
  namespace: analytics
spec:
  replicas: 2
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: reporter
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8080
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: "100m"
            memory: "128Mi"
          limits:
            cpu: "200m"
            memory: "256Mi"
```
## Verification Commands
```bash
kubectl apply -f limitrange.yaml
kubectl apply -f quota.yaml
kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml
kubectl describe resourcequota analytics-quo -n analytics
kubectl run overload-test --image=busybox --restart=Never --requests=cpu=500m,memory=600Mi --dry-run=server
```
## Rollback Strategy
```bash
kubectl delete -f quota.yaml
kubectl delete -f limitrange.yaml
kubectl scale deployment reporter --replicas=0 -n analytics
```

## Why This Is Asked
Tests the candidate's ability to compose namespace-scoped config reloads using standard primitives (InitContainers, sidecars, Secrets, PVCs, and NetworkPolicies) without custom operators, focusing on reliability and reload semantics.

## Key Concepts
- InitContainer bootstraps config from central API
- Sidecar monitors config changes and signals main app
- Secrets for API tokens and credentials
- Shared volume for config sync
- PVC for logs and /logs
- Namespace NetworkPolicy restricts egress to config API

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: config-reload
  namespace: <namespace>
spec:
  replicas: 1
  template:
    spec:
      volumes:
        - name: config
          emptyDir: {}
        - name: logs
          persistentVolumeClaim:
            claimName: logs-claim
      containers:
        - name: app
          image: your-app:latest
          volumeMounts:
            - name: config
              mountPath: /etc/app/config
            - name: logs
              mountPath: /var/log/app
        - name: reloader
          image: myorg/config-reloader:latest
          command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "while true; do sleep 300; done"]
          volumeMounts:
            - name: config
              mountPath: /etc/app/config
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you validate config before applying a hot reload?
- How would you handle partial reload failures or rollback?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked

This question tests practical CKAD skills: dynamic configuration via ConfigMaps, per-namespace isolation, InitContainers, health checks, logging, and network policy considerations.

## Key Concepts

- **Namespace-scoped ConfigMaps**: Enable dynamic feature flags without pod restarts
- **InitContainers**: Provide bootstrap tooling (curl) before the main container starts
- **Conditional sidecars**: Driven by ConfigMap values to enable canary deployments
- **Readiness and liveness probes**: Ensure controller and application health
- **PVC-backed logs**: Provide persistent storage for debugging and audit trails
- **NetworkPolicies**: Enforce zero-trust networking by restricting egress to known endpoints

## Trade-offs

| Aspect | Consideration |
|--------|----------------|
| **Polling Interval** | Frequent polls increase API load; infrequent polls delay flag propagation |
| **ConfigMap Updates** | Applications must watch or periodically read the ConfigMap to detect changes |
| **Sidecar Overhead** | Running a sidecar even when disabled consumes resources; consider whether the main container can react to flag changes directly |
| **Egress Restriction** | Locking down NetworkPolicy requires knowing all upstream dependencies upfront |
| **Log Persistence** | PVCs add operational complexity and cost; consider external logging solutions for production |

## Minimal YAML Skeleton

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: feature-flags
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: feature-flags
  namespace: feature-flags
data:
  flags.json: '{}'
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: logs-pvc
  namespace: feature-flags
spec:
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteOnce
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 1Gi
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: flag-poller
  namespace: feature-flags
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: flag-poller
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: flag-poller
    spec:
      initContainers:
        - name: install-curl
          image: curlimages/curl:latest
          command: ['sh', '-c', 'cp /usr/bin/curl /tools/curl']
          volumeMounts:
            - name: tools
              mountPath: /tools
      containers:
        - name: poller
          image: your-poller-image:latest
          command: ['/bin/sh', '-c', 'while true; do curl -s $FLAGS_API > /config/flags.json; sleep 60; done']
          volumeMounts:
            - name: config
              mountPath: /config
            - name: logs
              mountPath: /logs
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /ready
              port: 8080
            initialDelaySeconds: 5
            periodSeconds: 10
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /health
              port: 8080
            initialDelaySeconds: 15
            periodSeconds: 20
        - name: sidecar
          image: your-sidecar-image:latest
          env:
            - name: FEATURE_ENABLED
              valueFrom:
                configMapKeyRef:
                  name: feature-flags
                  key: enabled
          volumeMounts:
            - name: logs
              mountPath: /logs
      volumes:
        - name: config
          configMap:
            name: feature-flags
        - name: tools
          emptyDir: {}
        - name: logs
          persistentVolumeClaim:
            claimName: logs-pvc
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: flags-egress-policy
  namespace: feature-flags
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: flag-poller
  policyTypes:
    - Egress
  egress:
    - to:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels:
              app: flags-api
      ports:
        - protocol: TCP
          port: 8080
```

This design balances flexibility with operational simplicity, making it well-suited for Kubernetes feature management in multi-tenant environments.
